## Verdict on the two-folding idea

The two-folding idea is a disguised single folding. Below is the argument, then the one lemma I think matters next. I don't have a mechanism that meets your bar.

## Theorem: two foldings reduce to one

This is a theorem modulo routine checks.

**Setup.** A folding f: P → Q exists when P is tiled edge-to-edge by mirror-adjacent copies of Q. Let Γ_X be the group generated by reflections in the edge lines of X. Then a folding gives Γ_P ⊆ Γ_Q.

**Claim.** Suppose P is a simple polygon that folds onto Q₁ and onto Q₂, with interior tiling vertices at angles π/k. Then exactly one of these holds:

1. Γ₁ and Γ₂ have the same point group and commensurable lattices. Their join Γ₃ is then a discrete reflection group. Both obstructions become two colorings of the vertex classes of one finer tile Q₃.
2. No such P exists.

**Sketch.**

- Γ_P contains a rank-2 translation lattice. Three non-concurrent edge lines give two independent translations. A closed polygon cannot have all of its edge lines concurrent.
- Γ_P is discrete, so its lattice is a finite-index lattice in Γ₁ and in Γ₂.
- Discrete Euclidean reflection groups have only four types: rectangle, (π/2, π/4, π/4), (π/2, π/3, π/6), and equilateral.
- The 45° and 60° families share only the directions 0 and π/2. That forces P to be rectilinear with translations (aℤ)² inside cℤ × c√3ℤ. This is impossible.
- Rotated copies of the same family, such as a rotation by arctan(3/4), share no edge directions.
- Same-family groups with commensurable rational offsets generate a discrete finer group.

**Consequence.** Take each S→T lift t′ in P's development. The conjunction "t′ is excluded by f₁ or by f₂" is a residue condition on the vertex classes of Γ₃. That is endpoint arithmetic on one folding, and you report that approach as saturated. Different triangles add nothing new. Local or partial folds with straight fold lines inherit the same Γ_P containment, so they don't escape this either.

## What the folding category leaves open

This is a conditional implication.

Every folding mechanism needs a tile Q with three properties:

- One vertex A has angle π/n.
- Every non-A vertex of P's tiling is either a wall corner or a "transparent" vertex with angle π/k.
- Q satisfies no-return at A: no generalized billiard path runs from A back to A while avoiding the blocking vertices.

The four discrete types are exhausted. Your W ≥ 4n−2 and W ≥ 6n−4 bounds cover them, along with the 45-45-90 exclusion for W ≤ 23. So any sub-24 room built from a folding must use a **non-discrete** tile. One example is the isosceles triangle with angles (π/5, π/5, 3π/5): 10 copies form a full star at A, and the 3π/5 vertices must be walls.

That moves the question from lattice parity to the illumination theory of Veech surfaces. It isn't a new mechanism, and you excluded repackaging Veech enumeration. I'm flagging it because the theorem above forces it.

## The sharp lemma whose resolution changes the situation

Treat this as a conjecture or recollection to verify. It isn't established here.

**Lemma (dark-pair localization).** Let P be a rational simple polygon with translation surface X_P. Suppose (S, T) is a dark pair whose dark set contains every reflected lift of T. Then at least one of these holds:

- (a) T's lift is a **periodic point** of X_P. That means it has finite orbit under the affine group, or it is fixed by every element of the Veech group in the Veech case.
- (b) S and T project to the same point under some folding of P onto a lattice-family tile.

**Why it's decisive.**

- If the lemma holds, the second case is your exhausted triangle-assembly territory.
- In the first case, you can test non-arithmetic Veech rooms directly. In genus 2, Möller's theorem says the only periodic points are the Weierstrass points. That gives a finite candidate list per room, roughly 6 points instead of a continuum.
- The lemma rules out the bulk of non-lattice rooms by computation rather than search.
- If the lemma fails, the counterexample is itself a dark pair outside every folding. That is the new mechanism you're looking for.

My recollection is that Apisa and Wright have results tying non-illumination on translation surfaces to periodic points. Hubert, Schmoll, and Troubetzkoy have finiteness results for Veech surfaces. Check whether (a) or (b) is already a theorem before you spend effort on it.

## Decisive small test

1. Take the (π/5, π/5, 3π/5) triangle and its 10-copy star (a decagon).
2. Compute the Weierstrass points of the double-pentagon surface. List which of them project inside the star.
3. Pick a point S at the star center. For each Weierstrass candidate T, check saddle connections from A-preimages to T-preimages up to length L.

The test answers one thing: can a non-arithmetic tile have no-return at A?

- **Return exists:** Folding constructions below 24 walls are dead, by the theorem above.
- **No return:** You get a genuine non-lattice parity analogue. You then need wall counting to show that the 3π/5 corners cost fewer than 24 walls.

## Most likely fatal flaw

In the double-pentagon surface, every vertex preimage is likely to merge into a single cone point. A-to-A saddle connections then exist in abundance. That would make no-return at A false, so the test likely returns "dead."
